sections.label: Debating two Bills together
sections.summary: The proposal allows substantive debate on both Bills at the same time, with formal Second Reading of the MRA Bill still held.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Members would be welcome to raise questions or express their views on both Bills during this debate and we will still have the formal Second Reading of the MRA Bill to ensure that procedural requirements are dealt with.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: However, this proposal is to allow for the substantive debate on both Bills to take place at the same time to allow for concerns on the related subject matter to be captured cogently in a single debate.

sections.label: Aims of medical disciplinary system
sections.summary: The speaker says they agree with High Court Judges on three aims: uphold public interest, protect public confidence, and achieve general deterrence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: On this point, I would like to reiterate that we are in full agreement with the High Court Judges on several occasions who have pronounced the three main aims of a disciplinary system that regulates the ethical and professional behaviour of the medical profession.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: And they are: to uphold public interest – I think there really can be no doubt; second, to preserve and protect public confidence in the health system and the medical profession; and third, to achieve general deterrence in disciplinary outcomes such that other doctors are deterred from adopting unethical practices.

sections.label: Dr Lim Lian Arn fined
sections.summary: The SMC DT found Dr Lim Lian Arn guilty of failing to obtain informed consent; he pleaded guilty and was fined the maximum $100,000.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: To give one example, Members will recall the case of Dr Lim Lian Arn, where the SMC DT had found Dr Lim guilty of failing to obtain informed consent from his patient.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Dr Lim pleaded guilty to the charge and was fined the maximum of $100,000 by the DT.

sections.label: Dr Lim's conviction overturned
sections.summary: Dr Lim's conviction was overturned on appeal to the Court of Three Judges because the disciplinary threshold of professional misconduct was not satisfied.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Dr Lim's conviction was subsequently overturned on appeal to the Court of Three Judges, primarily on the basis that the disciplinary threshold of professional misconduct was not satisfied in that case.

sections.label: Survey on steroid injection practice
sections.summary: A survey showed fewer doctors gave the same steroid injection while median cost increased, which the speaker says affected practice behaviour to patients' detriment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Doing a survey on the number of doctors who gave the same steroid injection, it showed that the number of doctors who were prepared to and continued to give that same steroid injection, the H&L injection, came down – the number of doctors reduced, while the median cost of these same injections increased.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: That is something done in Singapore on a procedure which most doctors would tell you is fairly routine.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: This study has demonstrated how the uncertainty engendered by these uncertainties, the medico-legal cases, the outcomes, has affected practice behaviour to the detriment of patients.

sections.label: 2017 study on defensive medicine
sections.summary: A 2017 British Medical Journal study found protracted disciplinary proceedings were associated with increased defensive medicine in the form of avoidance behaviour.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: A 2017 study published in the British Medical Journal found that protracted disciplinary proceedings were associated with an increase in defensive medicine in the form of avoidance behaviour – the kind of behaviour that one might have seen after Lim Lian Arn's case, when fewer doctors were prepared to offer that treatment.

sections.label: Defensive medicine negative effects
sections.summary: A lecture assessed that more defensive medicine leads to poorer outcomes, including unnecessary procedures, higher costs, doctor stress and eroded trust.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In that lecture, it was assessed that an increase in the practice of defensive medicine leads to far poorer outcomes, with some of the negative effects being: (a) a rise in medical procedures which are not in the best interests of the patient – more investigation and more checks just to ensure that there could not be a suggestion that perhaps some other test ought to have been done for this patient; (b) rising insurance and hence medical costs – overall, an increase in cost to the detriment of patients and to society; (c) stress for doctors, which we have heard articulated to the work group on several occasions; and (d) finally, critically, an erosion of trust in the doctor-patient relationship.

sections.label: Work group appointment date
sections.summary: The work group was appointed in March 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The work group was appointed in March 2019.

sections.label: Engagements with doctors
sections.summary: The engagements sought to understand concerns about informed consent and the SMC disciplinary procedure, consulting more than 1,000 doctors.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: These engagements sought to understand the breadth and depth of concerns and issues with the taking of informed consent and with the SMC disciplinary procedure.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: They consulted more than 1,000 doctors of varying seniority from a range of diverse practices across the public and private healthcare settings.

sections.label: Work group report release
sections.summary: On 28 November 2019 the work group released a 100-page report of final recommendations, which the Government accepted.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: On 28 November 2019, the work group released its 100-page report setting out its final recommendations and also the background thinking to its recommendations and what it was proposing to do.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The Government subsequently accepted the recommendations and the contents of the work group's report ought to be considered by Members when debating these two Bills that are before us.

sections.label: Hii Chii Kok advice standard
sections.summary: In 2017 the Court of Appeal set the legal standard for a doctor's duty to advise in Hii Chii Kok v Ooi Peng Jin London Lucien.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In 2017, the Court of Appeal pronounced the current legal standard for the doctor's duty to advise in the case of Hii Chii Kok v Ooi Peng Jin London Lucien.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Under the Hii Chii Kok test, a doctor's duty to advise requires that he disclose to a patient information that is relevant and material when giving the patient medical advice.

sections.label: Government recalibrates medical advice test
sections.summary: After studying the recommendations, the Government accepted recalibrating the test for medical advice while preserving patient autonomy as in Hii Chii Kok.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: After studying the work group’s recommendations, the Government accepted the recommendation to recalibrate the test for medical advice in the way in which I had outlined earlier.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: On the one hand, this new test will strive to preserve the principle of patient autonomy as set out in Hii Chii Kok, by requiring healthcare professionals to give their patients the information they require to make an informed decision.

sections.label: Standard of care test
sections.summary: A healthcare professional meets the standard of care if accepted by peer medical opinion and that opinion is logical.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The test provides that a healthcare professional will meet the standard of care in giving medical advice to a patient where two conditions are satisfied.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: These two conditions are: First, he acts in a manner which is accepted by the medical opinion of a respectable body of such healthcare professionals as reasonable professional practice in the circumstances.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Second, this peer professional opinion has to be logical, in that it has compared and weighed the risks and benefits of the conduct in question and arrived at a defensible conclusion that is internally consistent and does not ignore known medical facts – a formulation that I am sure that many in this House would be familiar with.

sections.label: Information for informed decision
sections.summary: The professional must give information a typical patient in the same circumstances would reasonably require to decide on treatment or advice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The healthcare professional must give his patient information that a patient in the same circumstances, that is, a “typical” patient, would reasonably require to make an informed decision about whether to undergo a treatment or follow a particular piece of medical advice.

sections.label: Medical records review limits
sections.summary: This does not oblige professionals to review substantial volumes of NEHR records to find the patient's concerns or queries.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In relation to information that ought to be apparent from medical records, this is not intended to impose an obligation on healthcare professionals to review and go back into reviewing substantial volumes of medical records or voluminous medical history on the National Electronic Health Record or NEHR, in order to try and work out or ferret out what are the concerns or queries the patient might have.

sections.label: Reasonableness of reviewing records
sections.summary: Reasonableness governs access and whether the doctor ought to review past records, with record age as a factor.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The litmus test is that of reasonableness – both in terms of what the healthcare professional has reasonable access to and also whether in the circumstance of the case, the discussion with the patient, the context in which the patient is seeing the doctor, whether that creates a scenario where the doctor ought to reasonably review these past records.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: For instance, a factor that would go into the assessment of what is reasonable might well be the age of the medical records in question.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: So, it would not ordinarily appear to be reasonable for a healthcare professional to have to trawl through old microfilms and medical records going back 10 years, barring some exceptional circumstance.

sections.label: Refusing information to patient
sections.summary: A professional cannot refuse to provide information merely because he thinks advice or treatment is in the patient's best interests.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: On the other hand, we are also making clear that a healthcare professional cannot simply refuse to provide information to his patient, merely because he thinks that providing a particular piece of medical advice or undergoing a treatment is in the best interests of his patient.

sections.label: Revising ethical codes on consent
sections.summary: The Ethical Code and Ethical Guidelines of the Singapore Medical Council and Singapore Dental Council will be revised on informed consent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: For a start, we will be revising the Ethical Code and Ethical Guidelines or ECEG of both the Singapore Medical Council and Singapore Dental Council in respect of the issue of the taking of informed consent.

sections.label: Reviewing SMC ethical guidelines
sections.summary: The SMC Ethical Code and Ethical Guidelines will be reviewed and revised to match proposed amendments to the Civil Law Act and Medical Registration Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Steps will be taken to review and revise the SMC Ethical Code and Ethical Guidelines so that it is in-step with these latest proposed amendments both to the Civil Law Act as well as to the Medical Registration Act.

sections.label: Four objectives of complaint system
sections.summary: Four objectives are stated: improve quality and consistency, reduce delays, protect patients more effectively, and encourage amicable resolution and a less adversarial disciplinary process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The four objectives are: firstly, to improve the quality and consistency of processes and outcomes in the system; second, to reduce delays and facilitate a more expeditious resolution of complaints; third, to protect patients more effectively; and fourth, to encourage as far as possible, the amicable resolution of complaints and facilitate a less adversarial disciplinary process in the appropriate cases between patients and doctors.

sections.label: Appointment of Disciplinary Commission
sections.summary: New section 57 provides for the Minister to appoint an independent body known as the Disciplinary Commission.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: First, to further improve the quality of processes and outcomes, the new section 57 provides for the appointment by the Minister of an independent body to be known as the Disciplinary Commission or DC.

sections.label: UK Medical Practitioners Tribunal Service
sections.summary: The UK General Medical Council established its Medical Practitioners Tribunal Service in 2012 to separate investigation functions from adjudication of hearings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In the UK, the General Medical Council, which is the equivalent of the SMC, established their Medical Practitioners Tribunal Service in 2012, and the purpose of this was, amongst other things, to provide a clear separation between a GMC's investigation functions and the adjudication of hearings, which is similar to what we are proposing here.

sections.label: Composition of Disciplinary Tribunals
sections.summary: New section 58(1) provides that individual Disciplinary Tribunals will comprise two doctors and one legal professional.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The new section 58(1) provides that individual DTs will now comprise two doctors and one legal professional.

sections.label: Judge chairing Disciplinary Tribunal
sections.summary: New section 59 provides a mechanism for the President of the DC to apply to the Chief Justice for permission for a Judge or Judicial Commissioner to chair the DT.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The new section 59 provides a mechanism for the President of the DC in those cases, to apply to the Chief Justice for permission for a Judge or a Judicial Commissioner of the Supreme Court to chair the DT in those cases.

sections.label: SMC legal advisory unit
sections.summary: The SMC will establish a legal advisory and prosecution unit.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: For this purpose, the SMC will be establishing a legal advisory and prosecution unit.

sections.label: SMC referral decision, CC recommendations
sections.summary: The SMC decides whether a matter is referred to the DT, and the CC recommends whether a formal DT inquiry is needed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: To this end, the SMC will be responsible for the ultimate decision as to whether a matter will be referred to the DT or not.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The new section 46(6) provides that the CC will now make recommendations to the SMC as to whether there should be a formal inquiry by a DT.

sections.label: SMC referral decision final
sections.summary: The SMC's decision on whether to refer a case to the DT is final.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The decision of the SMC as to whether to refer a case to the DT will be final.

sections.label: Estimated case resolution time
sections.summary: An average case is estimated to take about 18 to 22 months to be resolved.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: On our estimate, on an average case, it would take something like a year and a half, 18 to about 20, 22 months for a case to be resolved and we believe that that is sufficiently reasonable time for the cases to be adequately disposed of.

sections.label: SMC complaint numbers
sections.summary: Since 2010 the SMC received about 165 complaints yearly, with roughly 10% reaching the DT.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Since 2010, in other words, for the past decade or so, the SMC has received an average of about 165 complaints every year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Each such complaint takes up considerable resources to manage, which will be better utilised for more deserving cases where the complaint actually has a good basis.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: And on our rough numbers, roughly about 10% of these complaints make it to the DT every year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: So, roughly about 16 to 18 cases make it to the DT.

sections.label: Review Committee replaces appeals
sections.summary: The Review Committee reviews CC decisions except referrals for formal inquiry, replacing appeals to the Minister for Health.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The Review Committee reviews the decisions of the CC except decisions to refer the complaint for a formal inquiry.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: This replaces the current appeals process whereby appeals against such decisions of CCs are made to the Minister for Health.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The new sections 54, 55 and 56 provide for the appointment of the RC to consider requests made by the complainant doctor or the SMC against the CC.

sections.label: RC majority and orders
sections.summary: The RC proceeds by majority and can order that the CC complied with procedural requirements or direct further investigations or inquiry.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The RC proceeds by majority and can make the orders such as stating that the CC has compiled with the procedural requirements, or it may direct the CC to conduct further investigations or inquiry.

sections.label: New complaint against doctor
sections.summary: Under section 50 subsections 6 and 7, the SMC may file a new complaint against a doctor based on the investigator's report.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: On the other hand, it may be a related matter, one which would be a matter of interest and in the current rules, you would have to restart the process just to look into that.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: So, in the end, it was decided that, to the extent that it is in respect of the same doctor or another doctor, the mechanism that is set out is in section 50, subsection 6 and 7 will apply, and the SMC may, on the basis of the report made by the investigator who has looked into these matters, file a new complaint against the doctor.

sections.label: SMC power on own motion
sections.summary: New section 59J(4) gives the SMC power to act on its own motion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The new section 59J(4) will, therefore, give the SMC power to do so on its own motion.

sections.label: SMC membership and standing changes
sections.summary: Elected SMC membership rises from 12 to 15, appointed falls from 15 to 12, and minimum standing drops from 10 to eight years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: As the leaders of the major medical professional bodies are elected into their roles, the elected membership in the SMC will, in effect, be increased from 12 up to 15 members whilst the appointed membership will be changed from 15 to 12 members.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In the same vein, the amended section 8 reduces the minimum years of standing required for a doctor to serve on the SMC from 10 years to eight years and a similar amendment has been made to the years of standing to allow a doctor to serve as a member on the Complaints Panel.

sections.label: Advisory and prosecution arms
sections.summary: The new unit has an advisory arm advising committees and a prosecution arm conducting prosecutions for the SMC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: To recap, it is the advisory arm of the new unit that will advise the various committees.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: But there will also be a prosecution arm of that new unit and this will conduct prosecutions on behalf of the SMC.

sections.label: In-house prosecution team
sections.summary: A dedicated in-house prosecution team within the SMC under the new unit will help strengthen SMC capabilities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: On the other hand, a dedicated in-house prosecution team, residing within the SMC under the new unit, will help SMC to strengthen its own capabilities.

sections.label: Reforms reflect strong ground sentiment
sections.summary: The speaker says the reforms are significant and reflect strong sentiment from doctors, patients and stakeholders consulted over many months.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: You have to look at it in its totality and I have not gone through every clause in detail.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: But I just want to end by saying that these reforms are significant.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: They reflect a very strong ground sentiment, both by doctors and patients, and the extensive work of the work group in consulting over so many months – the number of doctors they have seen, the number of patients the advocacy groups have seen.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: They have also touched on stakeholders – insurers, lawyers, practitioners.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: They represent a very strong sense of what the industry – the legal, medical fraternity – wants to see.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: And many of these amendments that we have made here reflect that sentiment.

sections.label: Work group report and recommendations
sections.summary: The work group was set up in March 2019 and by November had submitted a report with 29 recommendations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The work group was set up in March 2019, as the Minister shared, and, by November, it had submitted its comprehensive report which contained 29 recommendations.

sections.label: Section 37 test combines tests
sections.summary: The section 37 test appears to deliberately clarify the common law modified Montgomery test and combines the Bolam-Bolitho test with it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The section 37 test, which is the subject of the Bill, appears to be a deliberate clarification of the common law modified Montgomery test that it manifestly takes into account peer professional opinion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In that way, the section 37 test combines the previous Bolam-Bolitho test with the modified Montgomery test.

sections.label: Polyclinics and short consultations
sections.summary: The Government is building new polyclinics for higher caseloads and seniors, and outpatient consultations are ordinarily scheduled for roughly 10 minutes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Even as the Government is ramping up the building of new polyclinics in anticipation of higher caseloads and a growing population of seniors, my understanding is that there are potentially a large number of patients, and each outpatient consultation is ordinarily scheduled for around roughly 10 minutes.

sections.label: Request for section 37 illustrations
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Minister to consider more illustrations for section 37 and clear MOH guidelines, especially for polyclinic and team-setting doctors.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Although this concern was raised to the work group, there are no illustrations in section 37 to guide doctors in team settings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Also, may I request that the Minister consider more illustrations to interpret section 37 for better guidance, especially for doctors in polyclinic settings with limited consultation time and for doctors who work in team settings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Alternatively, or preferably in addition, could clear guidelines be issued by MOH as to how exactly doctors should practise in light of these constraints?

sections.label: Mandatory review of section 37
sections.summary: The speaker suggests a mandatory review in two or three years of the section 37 test and new disciplinary process, and more frequent reviews of informed consent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In line with this, I would also make another suggestion which was given to me in feedback by a doctor and that is to have a mandatory review perhaps in two or three years' time on how the section 37 test and the new disciplinary process have worked in practice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I would suggest that the Government review the issue of informed consent more frequently in light of the rapid changes in medicine, including the use of telemedicine and artificial intelligence-assisted medicine.

sections.label: Doctors supporting legislative changes
sections.summary: A doctor speaker says professional and personal thoughts of caring for someone's loved one connect humanity, and supports the broad architecture of the legislative changes.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: And for those of us who happen to be doctors as well, seeing it from the professional lens but, at the same time, having those thoughts go through our minds that the person we are caring for is someone's loved one – could be very much like our loved one; that humanity connecting us together.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: I support the broad architecture of the legislative changes.

sections.label: Statutory test superseding case law
sections.summary: The passage asks how often a statutory test is legislated so quickly to supersede case law after a high profile Court of Appeal judgment such as Hii Chii Kok.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: How often is a statutory test legislated so quickly to supersede case law after a high profile Court of Appeal judgment such as the case of Hii Chii Kok.

sections.label: Different peer professional opinions
sections.summary: The passage asks the Minister what approach will be taken under proposed section 37(4) when there are different peer professional opinions, each deemed reasonable and logical.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: On the proposed section 37, sub-section (4) can I ask the Minister what will be the approach when there are different peer professional opinions, each of them deemed reasonable and logical?

sections.label: Lowering minimum years for SMC
sections.summary: The passage says lowering the minimum years of standing from 10 to eight for the SMC sends a message of inclusion of younger doctors' views and experiences.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: It starts by touching the ground every day, all the time.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: I want to speak about younger doctors because for the SMC, lowering the minimum years of standing from 10 to eight, it sends an important message of inclusion – inclusion of the views and experiences of our younger doctors.

sections.label: Resident with drug allergy
sections.summary: The passage states that one of the 180 residents was a patient with a drug allergy newly diagnosed during a hospital admission.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: One of the 180 residents was a patient with a drug allergy, newly diagnosed during a hospital admission.

sections.label: State Coroner found nurse negligent
sections.summary: The passage states the State Coroner found staff nurse Mdm Leong negligent because by the legal definition there was a duty of care, breach and resulting harm.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: The State Coroner found staff nurse Mdm Leong negligent because by the legal definition of neglience, there was a duty of care, that care was breached for whatever reason and harm ensued as a result.

sections.label: Nurses Association home care
sections.summary: The then-executive director of the Singapore Nurses Association said a home has 180 elderly residents requiring a certain level of care.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: The then-executive director of the Singapore Nurses Association was quoted as saying, "This is a home with 180 elderly residents and they require a certain level of care.

sections.label: Healthcare workers and institutions duty
sections.summary: Healthcare workers as professionals must take responsibility, while healthcare institutions have a duty of care to make safer workplaces and reduce human errors.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Healthcare workers being professionals must necessarily take responsibility, but our healthcare institutions also have a duty of care and a role to play in making safer workplaces and reducing the risk of human errors.

sections.label: Patient-centric test for medical advice
sections.summary: Annex E states the new test is patient-centric, based on peer professional opinion, regarding patient autonomy and choice, and material to the patient.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In Annex E of the report, dealing with legal tests for the provision of medical advice, it spells out the motivation for the new test.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: It claims, "This is a patient-centric test based on peer professional opinion which has regard to patient autonomy and choice and takes into account what is material to the patient." This test is called a patient-centric test but in broad strokes, it moves the needle towards the weight of doctors.

sections.label: Calibration for medical advice question
sections.summary: The question asks how the proposed calibration for medical advice in favour of peer professional opinion improves on the status quo.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Can the hon Minister please tell how the proposed calibration for medical advice in favour of peer professional opinion represents an improvement on the status quo?

sections.label: Medical opinion sometimes irrelevant
sections.summary: Even with the new test, there remain instances when the body of medical opinion is irrelevant.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Even with this new test, there remains instances when the body of medical opinion is irrelevant.

sections.label: Role of medical opinion standard
sections.summary: Clarification is sought on whether the body of medical opinion still has a role as the standard of care in this area.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Here, may I seek clarification on whether there is still a role for the body of medical opinion to be the standard of care governing this area?

sections.label: Therapeutic privilege and doctors
sections.summary: Speaker cites a discussion with Dr Koh Poh Koon on doctors exercising therapeutic privilege and asks the Minister to clarify the new test's limits.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: At the same time, often, we need the doctor to help the patient.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I had an illuminating discussion with the hon Senior Minister of State for Health, Dr Koh Poh Koon at the Members' Room yesterday where he shared instances when he was in medical practice where he had to exercise therapeutic privilege, often at the instance of the patient's relatives and not provide his patients with information that may lead to this patient becoming paraylsed with fear and becoming unsure as to what to do.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: That would not be a good outcome for the patients.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: We therefore need to continue to support doctors who in good faith and with utmost competence and due diligence – act in the interests of patients.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: And this, in the words of the hon Minister, would enhance decision-making and better outcomes for patients.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I ask for the Minister to clarify how this is addressed by the new test, as well as to ask the hon Minister to spell out more clearly the limits of this test in matters of fact-finding vis-a-vis the patient.

sections.label: Bill's steps in right direction
sections.summary: The Bill enables immediate interim orders, specifies a statute of limitations, and sets timelines for investigation and disciplinary deliberations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Why is the Bill before us today a step in the right direction?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: These include firstly, it will enable the SMC to issue immediate interim orders against medical practitioners if there is imminent danger to the public.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Second, it specifies the statute of limitations which would tend to enhance clarity and confidence amongst the medical profession.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Thirdly, it specifies timelines for investigation and disciplinary deliberations such as, for example, that for the complaints panel to appoint an Inquiry Committee and for the Inquiry Committee to perform its filtering role.

sections.label: Statute of limitations and section 41
sections.summary: A six-year statute of limitations for complaints is a good step, but section 41(6)(3) may negate its whole point.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Next, Sir, while the introduction of a statute of limitations of six years for complaints is a good step to allow for the referral of a late complaint to the President of the Disciplinary Commission, section 41 (6)(3) may appear to negate the whole point of a statute of limitations.

sections.label: Lim Lian Arn and Soo Shuenn Chiang
sections.summary: In the Lim Lian Arn and Soo Shuenn Chiang cases, the Court of Three Judges found unjust outcomes arose from ignorance of the ECEG and medical ethics.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In the Lim Lian Arn and Soo Shuenn Chiang's cases, unjust outcomes were found by the Court of Three Judges to have arisen from ignorance of the Ethical Code and Ethical Guidelines or ECEG and of medical ethics in general.

sections.label: Commercial law firms' attitude
sections.summary: The 2019 work group observed that commercial law firms appear to seek convictions at all costs, sometimes disregarding the ECEG and past judgments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The 2019 work group observed that commercial law firms appear to have an attitude of securing convictions at all costs, even at the expense of disregarding the ECEG and previous Court of Three Judges judgments in some cases.

sections.label: SMC legal expenses and in-house units
sections.summary: In 2018 the SMC's net legal expenses for disciplinary proceedings were $880,000, and the 2019 work group recommended in-house prosecution and legal advisory units.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In 2018, the SMC's net legal expenses for disciplinary proceedings – 880,000 – comprised a significant 10% of total operating expenses of $8.8 million.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The 2019 work group report recommended the creation of in-house prosecution and legal advisory units to improve access to legal resources.

sections.label: DT members unpaid for case time
sections.summary: Complaints Panel members from the private sector receive a small honorarium, but DT members are not reimbursed for time on cases, and senior doctors block out about a week of clinical appointments per case.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Currently, while a small honorarium is paid to some Complaints Panel members from the private sector, DT members are not reimbursed for the time spent on working on a case.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The DT's two senior doctors would usually have to block out their clinical appointments for about a week for each DT case, representing a significant trade-off in respect of income.

sections.label: Support and resources for doctors
sections.summary: The speaker suggests the Government work with SMC to study better ways to incentivise and support doctors on Disciplinary Committees, and asks for assurance that sufficient resources will be dedicated to meet new MRA timelines.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: My suggestion here would be for the Government to work with SMC to study this problem and consider better ways to incentivise and support doctors serving and Disciplinary Committees, including considering non-monetary forms of recognition and the provision of better supporting resources.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Next Sir, I would like to ask if the Minister could provide assurance that sufficient resources will be dedicated to allow adherence to stipulate the timelines under this new MRA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: There is a perception that the SMC is stretched thinly on resources explaining the long timelines taken to resolve complaints and the existence of a significant backlog of cases.

sections.label: SMC concluded 18 of 138 complaints
sections.summary: Out of 138 complaints in 2018, SMC could only conclude 18 inquiries.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
sentences.text: For example, out of 138 complaints in 2018, SMC could only conclude 18 inquiries.

sections.label: New Inquiry Committee three-week decision
sections.summary: The new Inquiry Committee will decide within three weeks whether a complaint is valid from a doctor's point of view, and vexatious complaints will be rejected immediately.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
sentences.text: The new Inquiry Committee will decide within three weeks whether the complaint is valid from a doctor's point of view; vexatious complaints will be rejected immediately.

sections.label: SMC accumulated surplus $4.9 million
sections.summary: Based on the SMC's 2018 annual report, it had an accumulated surplus of $4.9 million as of 31 March 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
sentences.text: Based on the 2018 annual report of the SMC, it has an accumulated surplus of $4.9 million as of 31 March 2019.

sections.label: Proposed $300 annual doctor fee
sections.summary: With 11,461 fully registered doctors in Singapore as of 2018, the speaker suggests each doctor pay an additional $300 annual fee to SMC, contributing $3.4 million a year, as some cases take up to seven years to resolve.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
sentences.text: As of 2018, there were 11,461 fully registered doctors in Singapore and almost of half of them were specialists.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
sentences.text: What I am going to suggest next will not go well with the doctors, including the physician that will examine me at my next medical report or medical check-up.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
sentences.text: However, in the larger interest of Singaporeans, I will like to suggest each of the doctors pay an additional $300 annual fee to the SMC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
sentences.text: Three hundred dollars per year might be a small proportion of the doctor's annual income.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
sentences.text: But, it will contribute $3.4 million a year to SMC and that might cover the additional costs to better the complaints by the patients.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Some cases brought to the SMC has taken a long time to resolve.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: It has created agony for some patients and doctors who wait up to seven years for justice to see its day.

sections.label: Six committees in a case
sections.summary: A case may pass through up to six committees: Inquiry, Complaints, Review, Health, Interim Orders and Disciplinary Tribunal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: A given case may not pass through as many as six committees, the Inquiry Committee, Complaints Committee, Review Committee, Health Committee, Interim Orders Committee and Disciplinary Tribunal.

sections.label: Work group complaint figures
sections.summary: The work group says only 7% of SMC complaints were dismissed as frivolous or vexatious, and the proposal adds five weeks and two doctors for the other 93%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: According to the work group, only 7% of SMC complaints have been dismissed as frivolous or vexatious.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: For the other 93% of the cases, this new proposal adds five weeks and two doctors without actually changing the outcome.

sections.label: Singapore doctor-patient ratios compared
sections.summary: Singapore has 2.3 doctors per 1,000 patients, compared with 2.8 in the UK, 3.8 in the EU and 3.5 in the OECD.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The current doctor-patient ratio in Singapore is one doctor for every 444 patients or 2.3 doctors for every 1,000 patients.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: In comparison, there are 2.8 doctors for every 1,000 patients in the UK.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The European Union average ratio is 3.8 doctors for every 1,000 patients.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The OECD average ratio is 3.5 doctors for every 1,000 patients.

sections.label: Montgomery and Hii Chii Kok tests
sections.summary: The English Court of Appeal set out a doctor's advice duties in Montgomery in 2015, and the Singapore Court of Appeal identified three stages in Hii Chii Kok in 2018.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: In 2015, the English Court of Appeal articulated this modified test in a case called Montgomery, where it set out a doctor's duties in relation to giving patients advice was actually to properly inform patients of the treatment options and the risks involved.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: In 2018, in the Hii Chii Kok case, which I think the Minister mentioned as well, the Singapore Court of Appeal was faced with a similar issue and again, it identified clearly the three different stages of the medical process – diagnosis, medical advice and treatment – and said that a different test ought to apply when we are talking about the giving of medical advice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: In the Civil Law Act, what we have now is an amendment proposed specifically to alter the common law test in relation to medical advice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: It does not change the common law test in relation to diagnosis or treatment.

sections.label: Defensive medicine and costs
sections.summary: Doctors need not inform patients of inconceivable risks or give every textbook footnote, and defensive medicine raises costs without necessarily better outcomes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: You do not have to actually inform patients of inconceivable risks and you do not have to give every footnote in the textbook.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Defensive medicine is of course a concern because if doctors prescribe a range of expensive diagnostic tests, most of which do not yield any results and feel compelled to give detailed pros and cons, this is definitely going to raise medical costs for the patients without necessarily giving better outcomes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: So, to me, the test put forward by the amendment to the Civil Law Act is a sensible and practical one.

sections.label: Doctors' duty to inform
sections.summary: In making medical decisions, doctors have a duty to inform and give the patient enough information to make the right decision.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: In the making of medical decisions, the doctors' duty is to inform and give the patient enough information to make the right decision.

sections.label: Withholding details from patients
sections.summary: Doctors may withhold informed consent details from patients in denial who need urgent life-saving surgery, talking to family instead.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
sentences.text: Because they know their parents better, they know that if the parents were to hear about the "C" word, they will deny treatment, they will insist on going home, and I think the doctor also knows in this situation, that the patient will ultimately be harmed by refusing surgery, by going home where they have an acute abdominal situation.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
sentences.text: I think in this situation, it is where the doctor spends time talking to the family instead of maybe just the patient alone, to help the family to understand the context in which the decision has been made and why a surgery is necessary.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
sentences.text: There are times in which we withhold a lot of the details of informed consent with that particular patient who may be in denial but who needs surgery urgently to convince the person to go for life-saving surgery.

sections.label: Doctors' difficult decisions and professional opinion
sections.summary: The Bill retains the construct of professional value of opinion so doctors advocate for patients rather than acting defensively.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
sentences.text: I think if all of us here, with aged parents, put ourselves in the shoes of a son or a daughter knowing your parents will refuse surgery if they know about the full context of what they are going to go through for the next three hours under the anaesthesia, I think you understand what I mean by saying that there are situations in which the doctor must make a difficult decision to put himself, probably at professional risk for the sake of the patient.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
sentences.text: And this is why in this Bill, the construct of a professional value of opinion is still important.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
sentences.text: Even as we try and shift some of the focus to become more patient-centric, we hope that doctors will not take a defensive approach, but will still continue to advocate the benefits of patients.

sections.label: Informed consent and language barriers
sections.summary: The speaker hopes the Minister will look into drawing up guidelines for doctors to obtain informed consent where language barriers exist.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: An important area is in the area of consent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: I hope the Minister would look into how guidelines can be drawn up for doctors to obtain informed consent, especially in cases where language barriers can be a challenge.

sections.label: Dialect and local language staff
sections.summary: Every clinic should have at least one person on duty trained to speak different dialects and local languages with competency.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Every clinic should have at least one person on duty who is trained to speak in the different dialects and local languages with a certain level of competency.

sections.label: Considering patient profile in consent
sections.summary: The Ethical Code and Ethical Guidelines should emphasise that doctors consider a patient's profile when informing them about conditions and treatment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The doctor should also consider if such a patient is well-informed, educated or able to understand what is being communicated.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: It should be emphasised in the Ethical Code and Ethical Guidelines on informed consent that a doctor should consider his patient’s profile when informing them about their medical condition and treatment options.

sections.label: Estimated investigation conclusion time
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Minister to help the House understand the estimated time for an investigation to be concluded at present.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Can the Minister help the House to understand what is the estimated time for an investigation to be concluded at present?

sections.label: Defensive medicine harms patients and system
sections.summary: Defensive medicine is longstanding, bad for patients, professionals and the system, and hospital scan pick-up rates are under 10% versus 25% worldwide.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: And so, the problem of defensive medicine is a longstanding one.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: And as Minister Gan Kim Yong noted in this House last year, defensive medicine "will not only affect doctors, but ultimately compromise the quality of medical care, raising medical costs and harming patient welfare." In short, defensive medicine is bad – it is bad for the patient; it is bad for the healthcare professional and it is bad for the system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: From my understanding, the pick-up rate from these scans at the hospital has been less than 10% compared to around 25% in the best centres worldwide.

sections.label: Over-diagnosis and inappropriate procedures
sections.summary: In one country up to 99.9% of thyroid cancers found by ultrasound screening were over-diagnosis, and up to 20% of certain cardiovascular procedures were inappropriate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: In one country, it is estimated that up to 99.9% of thyroid cancers detected there by way of the aggressive use of ultrasound screening represented over-diagnosis.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: For certain cardiovascular procedures, up to 20% of the procedures ordered have been found to be inappropriate across various countries, despite clear and broadly accepted criteria for what is appropriate.

sections.label: Bills as back-stop preserving trust
sections.summary: The Bills' structures should be a back-stop when doctor-patient relationships break down, preventing lost trust from eroding the larger system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: The ultimate paradox for the enhancements in the Bills before us is that one hopes to never have to use these, for when these are invoked, it means a care relationship between doctor and patient has broken down.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: In such a situation, our structures and processes must become a back-stop, to serve justice efficiently and consistently.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: In turn, this prevents the loss of trust in one relationship from spilling over into and eroding the larger system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: All stakeholders – doctors, patients, the professional self-regulatory system, healthcare institutions – all of us need to work hard to maintain and grow this trust, because it is our surest way to guard against a regression into defensive medicine.

sections.label: Singapore medical complaint rates
sections.summary: Singapore has averaged 214 medical complaints against doctors yearly over five years, ranging 161 to 259, or 16 per 1,000 practitioners.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Currently in Singapore, there is a stable trend of medical complaints against doctors at an average of 214 cases per year over the last five years, range 161 to 259.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
sentences.text: This translates to 16 complaints per 1,000 medical practitioners.

sections.label: SMC disciplinary legal expenses
sections.summary: The SMC spent nearly $2 million in 2017 and $1.6 million in 2018 on legal expenses for disciplinary proceedings, and asks the estimated cost increase.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
sentences.text: According to SMC annual report, SMC spent nearly $2 million in 2017 and $1.6 million in 2018 for legal expenses for disciplinary proceedings.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
sentences.text: What is the estimated increase in running cost of the SMC when this legislation takes effect?

sections.label: Duty to review old records
sections.summary: An orthopaedic surgeon was liable for not reviewing old notes recording eczema, raising whether doctors must go through all old notes.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
sentences.text: In one of examples cited in the legislation stated by the Minister just now, it states that the doctors need to go through old medical records to sieve out information which may be material to the case.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
sentences.text: The orthopaedic surgeon is liable because the surgeon failed to look through the old notes which stated the patient had eczema recorded many years ago.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Is it the duty of the doctors to go through all old notes even stored in microfilm?

sentences.speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I know as a medical practitioner we are required by law to keep our medical records for seven years.

sections.label: Mediation and medical indemnity insurance
sections.summary: A Member asks whether the legislation can make mediation mandatory and require medical indemnity insurers to cover mediation costs, noting the Bill's Inquiry Committee.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Currently, our medical indemnity insurance covers doctors for medico-legal claims but I understand from some of my medical colleagues, the insurance companies are not obliged to accept mediation and may not pay for any cost involved in mediation.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Can this legislation make mediation mandatory and also make it mandatory for medical indemnity insurers to honour and cover the cost of mediation if mandated by SMC?

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: I note with interest in the Medical Registration (Amendment) Bill, the introduction of an Inquiry Committee in the proposed framework for the Singapore Medical Council’s Disciplinary Process as envisaged in the Bill.

sections.label: Costs against complainants
sections.summary: The Inquiry Committee and Complaints Committee have power to order costs against complainants to prevent frivolous and vexatious complaints.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: To prevent the filing of frivolous and vexatious complaints, the Inquiry Committee and the Complaints Committee also have power to order costs against the complainant.

sections.label: Complaint process stages and timelines
sections.summary: The Inquiry Committee's initial review is envisaged to take about five weeks, the Complaints Committee three to four months, before the Disciplinary Tribunal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: In this regard, I note that the first stage of the initial review and triage by the Inquiry Committee is envisaged to be completed within a general timeline of about five weeks.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The second stage of the inquiry by the Complaints Committee would take another three to four months to ascertain if the complaint proceeds on to the Disciplinary Tribunal, which is the third stage.

sections.label: Legal aid and Inquiry Committee resources
sections.summary: A Member suggests extending legal aid to laypersons and seeks assurance that adequate resources and manpower be provided upfront to the Inquiry Committee.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Perhaps legal aid access can also be extended and provided to laypersons who have legitimate complaints and require assistance to file complaints.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: I am very grateful to Minister Edwin Tong for his clarifications and I seek the Ministry's assurance that adequate resources and manpower be provided upfront to the Inquiry Committee to cater and address these complaints filed by complainants or their families and their next-of-kin quickly, efficiently, satisfactorily, because although they are looking for a lifeline, they cannot be made to wait a lifetime.

sections.label: Informed consent complaint numbers
sections.summary: Informed consent complaints averaged one per year from 2010 to 2016, five per year in 2017 and 2018, and 17 cases in 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: On informed consent complaints, there was an average of one per year from the years 2010 to 2016.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: It became five per year in 2017 and 2018 – roughly around the period of time that Hii Chii Kok was decided.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In 2019 alone last year, there were 17 cases – 17 cases filed in respect of alleged informed consent breaches and drop in standard.

sections.label: Perception and rising damages
sections.summary: The Member says perception has a tangible impact on how complaints are brought and that damages rose threefold in Singapore between 2017 and 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: But the point I am making is that the perception actually results in there being tangible impact in the way the complaints are brought, in the way that damages have gone up over the years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: And so, in Singapore, between 2017 and 2019, it is a threefold increase.

sections.label: Disciplinary Commission and training
sections.summary: A separate Disciplinary Commission was set up to ensure members on Complaints Committees, Disciplinary Tribunals and Review Committees are continually refreshed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Many of the Members have mentioned and we have made a commitment to training in perhaps the boldest possible way by setting up a separate body, the Disciplinary Commission (DC), to look specifically at training, to make sure that the members who sit on the Complaints Committees (CCs), on the Disciplinary Tribunals (DTs), on the Review Committees (RCs), on the many "Cs" that someone has spoken about, are all of sufficient standard and not just at one point in time but are continually refreshed.

sections.label: Answering patient questions and concerns
sections.summary: If a patient asks a question or expresses a view or concern, the doctor still has to answer it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I will come back to that in a moment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: But if a patient asks a question directly, expresses a view or a concern, then even if that view of concern might not be regarded by the peer professional test as being material in every consultation, that still has to be answered by the doctor.

sections.label: Relevance of old medical records
sections.summary: The passage states that relevance is situational and fact-specific, and older medical records are less likely to be relevant.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Because it is very situational, very fact-specific, fact-dependent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I hesitate even to say but probably the longer, further back a medical record is, the scan is – 10, 12, 15 years ago – the less likely it is to be relevant.

sections.label: Montgomery test and polyclinic caseload
sections.summary: The formulation would not add more on consultation time, and polyclinic caseload has been relatively steady in the past three to five years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: But on the current modified Montgomery test, I do not think this formulation would add more by way of the time that you take to consult.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I have also had a quick look at the polyclinic caseload over the years and I believe the numbers have been relatively steady in the past three to five years in terms of the caseload, roughly per consultant per day.

sections.label: Team-based care and consent
sections.summary: A Court decision stated that in public hospitals practising team-based care, other team members may explain risks and obtain consent on the surgeon's behalf.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: You have got to give the right information, you got to ensure that the patient understands and so on.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: There have been several cases, the most recent of which is the case involving Dr Yeo Tseng Tsai, a decision decided last year where the Courts commented and I would just quote from a small portion of it at paragraph 50 of the Judgment where the Court says that "...in a public hospital that practises team-based care, it is reasonable for other members of the operating surgeon's team to explain the risks of the proposed treatment and to obtain the patient's consent on the surgeon's behalf." And that is a point that is quite consistent across several other decisions in the High Court in Singapore.

sections.label: Orders used against two doctors
sections.summary: The orders are not made lightly and have been used twice recently, against Dr Wee and Dr Ler Teck Siang.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: So, we do need to give some degree of assessment on the ground.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: But to illustrate the point that these orders are not made lightly, Members may be aware that it has been used twice in recent times – one against Dr Wee when there was a Court decision in relation to his conduct, and there was also a case involving Dr Ler Teck Siang who was involved in the leak of data from a HIV registry.

sections.label: Complaints Panel non-doctor composition
sections.summary: The 50 non-doctors were 18 legal professionals and 32 lay persons.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The 50 non-doctors comprised 18 legal professionals and another 32 lay persons.

sections.label: SMC Complaints Panel targets
sections.summary: Once amendments are in force, the SMC intends at least 120 doctors and 60 lay persons and legal professionals on the Complaints Panel.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Moving forward, once the amendments are in force, the SMC intends to have minimally 120 doctors and 60 lay persons and legal professionals on the Complaints Panel.

sections.label: Complaint investigation timeframes
sections.summary: Cases at the CC average about 18 months, DT referrals add 23 months, and the SMC aims to complete the process in 18 to 22 months.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: How long does it take for the investigation to be concluded at present?

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: But over the last five years, based on data, the average time that it takes to conclude cases at the CC is about 18 months.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In fact, some take more time than this.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: And then cases referred to the DT take an additional 23 months.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: So, two more years on top of this.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: We are trying to put everything into a system where, on the average, between 18 and 20-22 months, we are able to complete the entire process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In terms of cases and backlog, the SMC has been working very hard to come up with a lot more resources and they have also used standing committees for the Complaints Committee and close to 90% of the stock of outstanding complaints as at September 2019 – that means all the complaints up to September 2019 – have been concluded by early September 2020.

sections.label: Honorarium for DT and CC
sections.summary: A DT member receives an $800 per day honorarium, while CC members receive a smaller amount given their lesser time commitment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Mr Perera may wish to know that, as of now, we already give an honorarium of $800 per day to a member of the DT.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: For members of the CC, there is also some amount but it is smaller, having regard to the fact that they play a lesser role in a sense that their time commitment is not as severe.

sections.label: SMC composition and representation
sections.summary: After the amendments, elected professional body representatives would outnumber Minister-appointed persons on the SMC, broadening medical representation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: On the SMC composition, I mentioned this at the outset, as it stands today, the number of persons nominated by the Minister has come down, and if you take into account the fact that the representation on the professional bodies, which are themselves elected by members of the medical profession – either the Academy of Medicine, College of Family Physicians Singapore or the SMA – then I think you will find that actually, after today's amendments, the cross representation and the spectrum of representation on the SMC of the medical fraternity is far broader and the numbers elected would outnumber the numbers appointed by the Minister.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I know that I would have omitted some and I beg the Members' indulgence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: We are prepared, after this Bill is passed, to take any of the further suggestions offline with the Members directly because the suggestions are good suggestions.
